newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt plans to avoid steps to stem trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt plans to avoid steps to stem trade gap.

text.p: The Czech government will avoid imposing import restrictions or exchange rate manipulations to help reverse a widening trade deficit, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Monday.

"A devaluation of the crown would generate acceleration of inflation and could trigger a loss of confidence in the government's economic policy with foreign investors and our citizens," Dlouhy told a trade conference.

"On the side of imports measures must not be taken which would be an obstacle to the liberalisation of imports, the government is not considering such intentions and will permanently speak against their application by other states."
Dlouhy repeated, in essence, previous statements that the government would attempt to decrease the trade gap, which reached a record 160 billion crowns last year, through more indirect means.
He said the government was working to establish an effective trade promotion organisation and was taking measures against imports of pirated goods.

Officials have repeatedly ruled out a currency devaluation or import surcharge as a cure for the trade problems, but many exporters and industrialists have called on the government to take direct steps to stem the trade deficit, which grew from 95.7 billion crowns in 1995.
Dlouhy said he expected the country to have a trade and current account deficit into the foreseeable future.
The current account deficit grew to $3.1 billion in the first three quarters of 1996, from a $684 million deficit in the first nine months of 1995.
The minister said that higher industrial output, which rose by a real 6.9 percent in 1996, could not cover high domestic demand which has led to the high level of imports.
Dlouhy said a real internal trade increase of 11.4 percent in the first 11 months of the last year, was faster than increases in real wages, suggesting less willingness for savings.
He said the government needed to encourage savings, which would help reduce demand for imports, but the promotion of private savings would require legislative changes of the social insurance system.
Under the current system, pension revenue from taxpayers are directly transferred to pensioners in a direct cash-flow operation, not into a trust fund as in many countries.
